**The SQ3R Strategy for Reading Textbooks**
The following is the SQ3R formula that will help improve your understanding, recall and retention of textbook material.
•	S = Survey the pages you plan to read.
•	Q = Question what you intend to take from your study session.
•	R3 = Read, Recall, and Review.

**Cornell System for Taking Notes**
The Cornell system for taking notes is designed to (1) save time while (2) enabling students to maximize the effectiveness of their notetaking. In this system there is no rewriting, revising or retyping of your notes once they've been made. The Cornell note taking system is sometimes referred to as the "Do it Right In The First Place" system. The Cornell system for taking notes consists of the following 3 steps and this specific page layout:

![cornell notes](https://pdfimages.wondershare.com/mobile-app/pdf-knowledage/cornel-note-taking.jpg)
Understanding how you Study - Modalities

**Prioritize your assignments**
Start the habit of beginning your studying with the most difficult, or important task first. Tackling the hardest task first, while you're still fresh and energized, will make the remainder of your studies much easier.

**Find a dedicated study space **
A key to ongoing time management is to find a dedicated study space free from distractions where you can concentrate. If you want to change up your study space, that's fine, just make sure to find a study space that works and stick with it.

**Create blocks of study time**
You should have dedicated study time–blocks of time where you focus on your studies. Blocks around 40 to 50 minutes are ideal, It's okay to take study breaks during your blocks for a snack, or just to get up and walk around, but make sure to return to your studies

**Schedule activities for after your school work.**
 One of the most difficult, yet important, elements of effective time management is to put your course work first. Complete your course work as soon as possible. Putting off less important activities until after you complete your course work will allow you stay on track and focus on your "fun" activities without the pressure looming course work.

CFItems.fullStatement:
**Step 1. Survey**
Before reading your text, get a general idea of the main themes, topics and concepts by skimming through the text or chapters. Identify and read the chapter headings, subheadings or introductions. Notice any graphics, such as charts, maps or other diagrams. Read the chapter summaries and conclusions. Try to develop an idea of what the author is going to say and communicate.
* Surveying the text provides your reading with focus and direction.
* Helps you develop an idea of what you'll be reading.
* Allows you to anticipate the text.

**Step 2. Questions**
As you survey the text, turn chapter headings and subheadings into questions. For example, the heading "Causes of World War II" changes to "What are the primary factors that led World War II?" Turning chapter headings and subheadings into questions provides direction for your reading and keeps you engaged. When your mind is actively search for answers as you read, you stay engaged.
* Write out the questions you develop from chapter headings.
* Examine the questions to find the direction of the text.
* Try to develop plausible answers to these question before reading.
* Attempt to answer these questions as you read.

**Step 3. Read**
Now that you've surveyed the text and developed a set of questions, read the text paying close attention to the direction of the text keeping in mind the information you already know and that you want to discover. As you read you may find the need to develop additional questions.
* Read for meaning and understanding.
* Seek to answer the set-up questions you developed in the previous step.
* Take notes in the margins or on a separate piece of paper.
* Take breaks if necessary.

**Step 4. Recall**
Recall is one of the most important steps for comprehending, mastering and retaining information from textbooks. More time should be spent on recall than reading itself. Without referring to your notes or your textbook, immediately after completing each section of reading, develop in your own words a summary of what you read, highlighting the most important topics, concepts and themes. Recite your summary to yourself or someone else.

**Step 1 - Divide your paper into two columns**
Use a large loose-leaf notebook for your notetaking. Only use one side of each leaf of paper in the notebook .Draw a vertical line 2 1/2 inches from the left side of your paper. This is the recall column of your notes. All your  notes will be taken to the right of this margin. Later, keywords or phrases can be written in the recall (left) column.
![cornell notes](https://pdfimages.wondershare.com/mobile-app/pdf-knowledage/cornel-note-taking.jpg)
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Divide your paper into two columns

CFItems.fullStatement:
**Step 2 - Take notes in the note-taking column**
Record notes in paragraph form in the note-taking column to the right. Capture general ideas and concepts, not illustrative ideas. Skip lines to show end of ideas or thoughts. Try to avoid long sentences. Using abbreviations will save time. Write as legibly as possible. Note down relevant questions and keywords in the recall (left) column to assist with future reviews of your notes.

![cornell notes](https://pdfimages.wondershare.com/mobile-app/pdf-knowledage/cornel-note-taking.jpg)
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Take notes in the note-taking column

CFItems.fullStatement:
**Step 3 - Review your notes within 24 hours**
After each reading read through your notes and make them more legible if necessary. Now use the 2 1/2 inches column to the left of your notes. Jot down ideas or keywords which give you the idea of the reading. (REDUCE) You will have to reread the ideas, reflect and put them in your own words if you can. Cover up the right-hand portion of your notes and recite the general ideas and concepts of the reading from memory. Overlap your notes showing only recall columns and use this for your review.

![cornell notes](https://pdfimages.wondershare.com/mobile-app/pdf-knowledage/cornel-note-taking.jpg)

CFItems.fullStatement: Take a screen shot

Elimination 
* Eliminate obviously wrong answer choices
* Eliminate choices that are **_partly_** correct
* Eliminate items that are correct but don’t answer the question

Sometimes it is a good idea to read the answers ***before*** answering a question. 
* Makes it easier to identify wrong answers when you then read/solve the problem
* Leads you to a strategy, saving you time you might lose trying inappropriate strategies
* Math word problems involving multi-step calculations

•	Read and process the entire question before reading the answer choices.
•	Read and think about each option separately. Do not group the choices. 
•	Make each option into a question that you can answer with:
•	          “Yes” or “No”
•	          “Applies” or “Does not apply”  
•           “True” or “False”

Examine a writing prompt before beginning a constructed response:
* Circle all verbs that describe what you are being asked to do
* Underline the words that describe what the task is
* Create a Do/What chart to generate and organize ideas



|Do (Verbs)  | What (Tasks) |
| -------- | -------- |
|      Enter Do Word      |     Enter Task Words      |

CFItems.fullStatement: Microsoft Word: Creating, Editing, Saving and Printing

Steps to Saving a Word document

1.	Make sure your **document** is open. ...
2.	Find the "**File**" tab and click on it. ...
3.	Click "**Save**" or "**Save As**". ...
4.	Under "**Save As**", decide on your **save** location. ...
5.	Double-click your save location. ...
6.	In the "**File Name**" field, type in your preferred **file** name.
7.	Click "**Save**" to save your file.
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Steps to Saving a Word document

CFItems.fullStatement:
**Steps to printing a Word document**
Open or create a Microsoft Word document. To do so, click on the blue app with a white document icon and bold "W," then click on **File** in the menu bar at the upper-left of the screen.

1.	Click on **File**
2.	Click on **Print**
3.	Select your printing option
4.	Click on Print or OK
1.	Make sure your **document** is open
2.	Find the "**File**" tab and click on it
3.	Click "**Save**" or "**Save As**"
4.	 Under "**Save As**", decide on your save location
5.	Double-click your save location
6.	In the "**File Name**" field, type in your preferred file name
7.	Click "**Save**" to save your file
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Steps to printing a Word document

CFItems.fullStatement:
Steps to inserting a photo into a word document
1.	Open the Word document that you want to insert a photo in.
2.	Click the place in your document where you want the picture to appear. 
3.	Access the **Insert Picture** dialog box (under the **Insert menu** option and ribbon)
4.	Browse to the photo you want to insert
5.	Click the **File**, then click Insert
6.	Modify the picture as necessary

How to insert an screen shot image 
1.	In the Word document, select **Insert** tab
2.	Click **Screenshot**
3.	From the drop down menu select **either take a screenshot of a window open on your computer or take a screen clipping of a portion of the screen**
4.	The screenshot or screen clipping will insert into your Word document
5.	**Adjust** sizing and placement as needed
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Steps to inserting a Image into a word document

CFItems.fullStatement:
**Insert text boxes**
1.	 Select the *Insert* ribbon menu tab,
2.	 Click the **Text Box** command in the **Text** group
3.	A drop-down menu will appear
4.	Click, hold, and drag to create the **text box**
5.	The insertion point will appear inside the **text box**

How to convert a paper document to a Word document
1.	Scan a document to a PDF, make sure your scanned document is saved as a PDF
2.	Open the PDF in word
	Windows – right click the PDF, select open window and click word from pop-out menu	
3.	Click OK when prompted, word will begin converting scanned PDF into a word document
4.	Enable editing for the file if needed. If you see a yellow bar with a warning at the top of the word window, click enable editing in the yellow bar in order to unlock the file for editing.
5.	Clean up the document. Check for missing words, remove any excess spaces and fix typos before document is ready to go.
6.	Save the document
CFItems.abbreviatedStatement: Convert scanned document to Word format

CFItems.fullStatement:
* Use flashcards to learn new words
* Try to visualize things you hear, or things read to you
* Write down key words, ideas or instructions
* Draw pictures to help explain new concepts and then explain the pictures
* Color code your notes, vocabulary words and textbook
* Be sure to read diagrams, maps and visuals that go along with the text
* Avoid distractions during study times
* Use outlines and concept maps to organize your notes
* Take note during lectures
* Study in silence often noise will distract you when you need to see things to remember them

* Find a study buddy
* Record class lectures
* Participate in class discussions as much as possible
* Have your hearing checked on a regular basis
* Use flashcards to learn new words; read them out loud
* Record yourself reading key terms and their definitions and then listen to the recording
* Study new material by reading it out loud
* Repeat facts with your eyes closed
* Read assignments out loud

* Learn by teaching
* Study in short blocks of time
* Use memory games
* Use a smart pen for taking notes
* Role-playing
* Study with others
* Participate in activities that involve touching, building, moving or drawing
* Do lots of hands on activities like completing art projects, taking walks, or acting out stories
* Take note – writing can help you retain information
* It’s ok to chew gum, walk around or rock in a chair while reading or studying
* Use flashcard and arrange then into groups to show relationships between ideas
* Take frequent, but not too long breaks while studying
* It’s ok to tap a pencil, shake your foot or hold on to something while you study
* Use a computer to reinforce learning through the sense of touch
* Remember you learn best by doing, not just by seeing, hearing or reading.
*
Study daily
Take regular breaks – like 5 minutes every half hour
Study in a way that suits your learning style
Study early – don’t put it off until the last minute
Study the hardest things first then move on to the easier ones
Spend the most time on the things you find difficult
Ask for help if you are struggling with something
Take notes and put things into your own words
Organize your notes in a notebook or folder
Look at your notes on a regular basis
Make connections between the topics you are studying and the topics you already know
Take practice tests so you are familiar with format
Keep track of your study progress in a notebook or using an online program
Quiz yourself about what you just studied
Congratulate yourself after a good study session

Educated Guess
* ***Educated guessing*** means using everything you know to attempt to answer the question.
* A **_random guess_** gives you a 25% chance of getting the right answer 
* An **_educated guess_** gives you a chance of answering correctly up to 75%.

Answers with the following words are usually wrong or false:
All		Always	Entirely	Must
None 		Every		Never		Worst
Only		Everyone

Answers with the following words are usually correct/true:
* Some		
* Sometimes	
* Generally	
* Usually	
* Frequently	
* Many		
* Probably	
* Most
* Often		
* Few		
* Seldom

* The context of a word includes all of the words and sentences that surround it and the situations in which the word is used. 
* When the answer is not clear, look for clues (context, tense, word type, grammar) in the question and the answer choices.

What’s the BIG IDEA?
* First and last sentences in a question
* Events, people, problems found in a passage
* Headings used in multi-paragraph articles
* The author’s intent in a passage

* Indicates more than one answer may be correct.

Have you ever read a question and thought you knew the answer, but then you read the answer choices and got confused? Try this!
* Cover up the answers and read the question, giving yourself a few seconds to let the answer come. 
* Then, once you’ve thought through your answer, read the answer choices, and select the answer that **best** matches your idea.
